title: Emraan Hashmi Walks Back Into the Dark. 'Rooh' Is the Horror Comeback His Fans Have Begged For — This Time, It Sings.
excerpt: A frost-covered forest, a girl levitating in mid-air, and two eyes that go completely black. The motion teaser for the horror-musical Rooh dropped on June 23 — and the serial killer of the genre is back.
body:
The teaser opens the way every great Emraan Hashmi horror film does — in the cold. An ember-lit forest, fog crawling between the trees, and a young girl suspended in mid-air, her body hanging where no body should hang. A hand wipes frost from a pane of glass. The camera tightens. And there they are: **Emraan Hashmi**'s eyes, the most reliable jump-scare in two decades of Indian horror, going slowly, completely black. "When a legend revisits the darkness," the tagline reads, "a nightmare is born."

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=Kju93XDiwR4</youtube>

He's back. After five years away from the genre that built him, Hashmi headlines **Rooh**, a self-described "high-concept musical-horror spectacle" announced on June 23 by producers Vikram Khakhar and Sunny Khanna of Vicked Films. And if you grew up watching *Raaz 3* through your fingers in a packed single-screen, the news lands somewhere between nostalgia and a shiver down the spine.

Let's be honest about why this matters. For a whole generation of Indian filmgoers, Emraan Hashmi *is* the horror movie. *Raaz: The Mystery Continues*, *Raaz 3*, *Ek Thi Daayan*, *Raaz Reboot* — he turned the haunted-mansion thriller into a box-office machine, all smouldering close-ups and songs you couldn't shake. Then the genre drifted, the franchise sputtered out with the pandemic-buried *Dybbuk* in 2021, and Hashmi reinvented himself as the sharp character actor of *Tiger 3* and *Showtime*. Rooh is him coming home.

> "Rooh is a film that immediately connected with me because it brings together new-age horror, emotion and music in a very powerful way. This is a space that audiences have always associated with me." — Emraan Hashmi

The "music" part is the twist worth leaning into. Hashmi's horror legacy was always half soundtrack — those aching, chart-topping ballads were as much the draw as the scares. Branding Rooh a *musical*-horror feels less like a gimmick and more like the film knowing exactly what made the originals tick. The man didn't just scare you; he serenaded you while doing it.

The pedigree behind the camera is the genuinely intriguing bit. Rooh is directed by **Mayank Sharma**, creator of Prime Video's acclaimed *Breathe* franchise — a filmmaker known for psychological dread and character-led tension rather than cheap fog and a screaming violin. He co-writes with **Vishal Kapoor**, whose credits include the unsettling *Lapachhapi* and *Chhorii*. That's a horror brain-trust that actually understands atmosphere. "Rooh is my attempt to create a film that goes beyond fear," Sharma said. "It's emotionally layered and immersed with unsettling atmosphere."

The ambition is unmistakable. Rooh is being built as a theatrical event, not an OTT drop — designed for the big screen, the big sound system, the collective gasp. And it's going pan-Indian from the start, releasing in **Hindi, Tamil and Telugu** in 2027. That three-language strategy is the smart new playbook (see *Toxic*, see *The Paradise*), and it signals the makers think they have something that travels well beyond the Hindi belt.

For the diaspora, that 2027 theatrical-first plan is the headline. Hashmi's horror films were a staple of NRI weekend cinema runs — the kind of movie you dragged your cousins to in Edison or Southall or Brampton because it was genuinely *fun* to scream together. A theatrical release means Rooh will almost certainly land in US, UK and Canadian multiplexes through the usual desi distributors before it ever streams. Bookmark it; this is a watch-it-with-a-crowd film, not a watch-it-alone-on-your-laptop one.

There are gaps, of course. No leading lady has been announced, no release date pinned beyond "2027," no plot beyond that levitating-girl tease. And Hashmi is a busy man — *Awarapan 2*, the Mohit Suri-produced sequel directed by Nitin Kakkar with Randeep Hooda and Disha Patani, is also on his slate. But that's the fun of an announcement like this. Right now Rooh is pure mood: frost, fire, black eyes and a promise.

Here's the take. Indian horror has been having a quiet renaissance — *Stree*, *Munjya*, *Chhorii* all proved audiences are hungry for it again. Putting the genre's most bankable face back in the centre of the frame, handed to a director who can actually build dread, with songs woven into the scares? That's not a comeback. That's a coronation waiting to happen. Two years is a long time to wait for a nightmare. We're already counting.
